## Purpose

This report demonstrates a complete binary logistic regression workflow. We will use the titanic data set which includes the demographics of passengers of the Titanic.

Our objectives are to:

1.  **Specify and estimate** several plausible competing binary logistic regression models using `glmmTMB`.

2.  **Compare nested models** using likelihood-ratio tests (χ²).

3.  **Evaluate overall model fit** using AIC and BIC.

4.  **Examine model diagnostics** and assess assumptions relevant to binary logistic regression.

5.  **Select and interpret** a preferred model, including transforming log-odds coefficients into odds ratios.

6.  **Report results reproducibly** using tables, figures, and Quarto.


```{r, setup}
library(glmmTMB)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(broom.mixed)
library(performance)
library(gt)
library(readr)
library(DHARMa)
library(ggeffects)
library(titanic)

titanic <- titanic_train

#Keep the same complete-case sample for every model
titanic <- titanic |>
  select(Survived, Sex, Age, Pclass) |>
  drop_na() |>
  mutate(
    Sex.Binary = case_when(
      Sex == "male" ~ 0,
      Sex == "female" ~ 1)) |>
  mutate(
    Survived.Char = case_when(
      Survived == 0 ~ "Died",
      Survived == 1 ~ "Survived")) |>
  mutate(
    Pclass.Char = case_when(
      Pclass == "1" ~ "First Class",
      Pclass == "2" ~ "Second Class",
      Pclass == "3" ~ "Third Class")) |>
  mutate(Pclass = factor(Pclass, levels = c(1, 2, 3))) |>
  select(Survived, Survived.Char, Sex, Sex.Binary, Pclass, Pclass.Char, Age)

n <- nrow(titanic)
```



This dataset contains data on **714 passengers**. The binary outcome variable is `Survived`: whether the passenger survived or died in the Titanic crash. Several other variables summarize characteristics of the Titanic passengers that could influence survival.

For this lab, we will focus on four variables:

|  |  |  |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| **Variable** | **Description** | **Role** |
| Survived | Whether a passenger survived or died in the crash | Outcome |
| Sex | Sex reported on legal documents | Predictor |
| Age | Self-reported age | Predictor |
| Pclass | What type of ticket was purchased; our proxy for socioeconomic status (SES) | Predictor |

## 1. Exploring the Data

```{r, descriptives}

descriptives <- titanic |>
  summarise(
    across(
      c(Age),
      list(mean = mean, sd = sd, min = min, max = max)
    )
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    everything(),
    names_to = c("variable", ".value"),
    names_sep = "_"

descriptives |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(columns = where(is.numeric), decimals = 2)
```

```{r, Age table}

titanic |>
  summarise(Mean = mean(Age), SD = sd(Age), Min = min(Age), Max = max(Age)) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(title = "Descriptive Statistics for Age") |>
  fmt_number(decimals = 2)
```

```{r, Survived counts table}
titanic |> count(Survived.Char) |> gt() |> tab_header(title = "Survival")

```

```{r, Sex counts}
titanic |> count(Sex) |> gt() |> tab_header(title = "Sex")
```

```{r, Class counts}

titanic |> count(Pclass.Char) |> gt() |> tab_header(title = "Ticket Class")
```
### Discussion
The 714 passengers ranged in age from months old children to 80 years, with an average age of about 30. None of the categorical variables were evenly distributed. More passengers died than survived, and about a third of passengers were male. Ticket class was also unbalanced: about half of passengers held third-class tickets, while first and second class were similar in size. The patterns of this data are as I would expect and is consistent with what I have heard about the titanic: a high number of deaths, more male than female passengers, and a large number of third class passengers.

## 2. Specifying competing binary logistic regression models

### My predictions
Based on what I saw in the movie, it seems like women and children were prioritized so I would expect female passengers to have higher odds of survival and children to have hgiher odds of survival. Also based on the movie, the lower class passengers were in the lower floors, far away from the lifeboats area. I predict that first and second class passengers would have higher odds at surviving compared to the third class passengers.

```{r, 2.2 model fit}
mod0 <- glmmTMB(Survived ~ 1,
  data = titanic, family = binomial(link = "logit"))

mod1 <- glmmTMB(Survived ~ Sex.Binary,
  data = titanic, family = binomial(link = "logit"))

mod2 <- glmmTMB(Survived ~ Sex.Binary + Pclass,
  data = titanic, family = binomial(link = "logit"))

mod3 <- glmmTMB(Survived ~ Sex.Binary + Pclass + Age,
  data = titanic, family = binomial(link = "logit"))
```

### Discussion
The intercept represents the log-odds of survival for the reference passenger, and who that passenger is changes as predictors are added. In mod1, the intercept (-1.35) is the log-odds of survival for male passengers, corresponding to a survival probability of about 21% (by using the plogis function), without accounting for class or age. In mod2, the intercept (-0.24) represents male passengers in first class, corresponding to a probability of about 44%. It is higher than in mod1 because first-class men survived much more often than men overall. In mod3, the intercept (1.25) represents a male first-class passenger aged 0, corresponding to a probability of about 78%. Because age is continuous and its coefficient is negative, setting age to 0 projects survival well beyond the observed data, so mod3 intercept has no meaningful interpretation on its own and serves mainly as a baseline from which the effects of sex, class and age are added.

## 3. Compare the models
```{r, anova tests}

tests <- anova(mod0, mod1, mod2, mod3)

tests
```

```{r, prepare tests}

tests <- tests |>
  mutate(`Residual df` = n - Df) |>
  select(`Residual df`, Chisq, `Chi Df`, `Pr(>Chisq)`) |>
  rename(
    Nested.df = `Chi Df`,
    Nested.Chisq.stat = Chisq,
    Nested.p.value = `Pr(>Chisq)`)
```

```{r, extract model metrics}

glance0 <- broom.mixed::glance(mod0)
glance1 <- broom.mixed::glance(mod1)
glance2 <- broom.mixed::glance(mod2)
glance3 <- broom.mixed::glance(mod3)
```

```{r, combine model metrics}

mods <- c(
  "mod0: Null",
  "mod1: Sex",
  "mod2: + Pclass",
  "mod3: + Age")

glances <- rbind(
  glance0,
  glance1,
  glance2,
  glance3)
```

```{r, combine comparisons}

comparison_table <- cbind(
  Model = mods,
  glances,
  tests)
```

```{r, model comparison table}

comparison_table |>
  select(
    Model,
    AIC,
    BIC,
    logLik,
    deviance,
    df.residual,
    Nested.df,
    Nested.Chisq.stat,
    Nested.p.value
  ) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(
    Model = "Model",
    AIC = "AIC",
    BIC = "BIC",
    logLik = "Log-likelihood",
    deviance = "Deviance",
    df.residual = "Residual.df",
    Nested.df = "Nested df",
    Nested.Chisq.stat = "Nested χ²",
    Nested.p.value = "Nested p"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(
      AIC,
      BIC,
      logLik,
      deviance,
      Nested.Chisq.stat
    ),
    decimals = 3
  ) |>
  fmt(
    columns = Nested.p.value,
    fns = function(x) {
      ifelse(
        is.na(x),
        "—",
        ifelse(x < .001, "< .001", sprintf("%.3f", x))
      )
    }
  ) |>
  sub_missing(
    columns = c(Nested.df, Nested.Chisq.stat),
    missing_text = "—"
  )
```
### Discussion
mod3 (sex, ticket class and age) provides the best fit to the data, with the lowest AIC and BIC of the four models. Both AIC and BIC decreased with each added predictor, with the largest drop occurring when sex was added to the null model, followed by smaller decreases for ticket class and then age. The likelihood-ratio tests showed that each addition significantly improved model fit: sex improved on the intercept-only model, ticket class improved on sex alone, and age improved on sex and class. AIC and BIC supported the same conclusions as the likelihood-ratio tests. 

Sex was the strongest predictor of survival, while ticket class and age each made smaller but meaningful additional contributions.

## 4. Evaluate binary logistic regression diagnostics

```{r, select model}
selected_row <- comparison_table |>
  filter(Nested.p.value < .05) |>
  slice_tail(n = 1)

#creating an object with our selected model's name for dynamic reporting
selected_name <- selected_row$Model

#case matching for dynamic reporting
selected_model <- switch(
  selected_name,
  "mod0: Null" = mod0,
  "mod1: Sex" = mod1,
  "mod2: + Pclass" = mod2,
  "mod3: + Age" = mod3)
```

The provisionally selected model is **`r selected_name`**.

Its performance is:

- AIC = **`r round(AIC(selected_model), 3)`**
- BIC = **`r round(BIC(selected_model), 3)`**

### Linearity on the logit scale

```{r, dharma sim}
#| echo: true
set.seed(9041)
res_mod3 <- simulateResiduals(mod3, n = 500, plot = FALSE)
```

```{r, dharma plot}
#| fig-height: 5.6
#| echo: false
plot(res_mod3)
```

### Collinearity

```{r, vif}
#| echo: false
check_collinearity(mod3)
```

```{r, vif plot}
#| echo: false
vif_plot <- plot(check_collinearity(mod3))
```


### Influence

```{r, outliers}
testOutliers(res_mod3)
```

### Events per predictor

```{r, epv}
#| echo: false
n_event <- sum(titanic$Survived == 1)
n_nonevent <- sum(titanic$Survived == 0)
n_coef <- length(fixef(mod3)$cond)
```

Here we have `r n_event` survivors and `r n_nonevent` passengers who died, with `r n_coef` coefficients in `mod3`.

### Discussion
Diagnostics for mod3 suggested that the model’s assumptions were largely satisfied. The DHARMa Q-Q plot showed residuals closely following the expected uniform distribution (KS test p = .90), with no evidence of over- or underdispersion (p = .81). In the residuals-versus-predicted plot, the upper quantile curve deviated from its expected value among passengers with the lowest predicted survival, suggesting that the model slightly underestimates survival for this group. 
Collinearity was low, there was no evidence of complete separation, and the outlier test identified only one extreme residual, fewer than expected by chance (p = .54). Overall, these diagnostics support the use of mod3.

## 5. Selecting and Reporting preferred model

I selected mod3 (sex, ticket class and age) as the preferred model. Each successive predictor produced a statistically significant improvement in model fit according to the likelihood-ratio tests, and mod3 had the lowest AIC and BIC of the four models.  Although mod3 is the most complex model, it includes only three predictors, and each corresponds to a substantive hypothesis about how passengers were prioritized during the evacuation. The diagnostics showed no serious problems: collinearity was low, there was no evidence of separation or influential observations, and there were ample events per coefficient. 

```{r, extract results}

coefficient_results <- broom.mixed::tidy(
  selected_model,
  effects = "fixed",
  component = "cond",
  conf.int = TRUE,
  conf.level = 0.95)
```

```{r, table coefficients}

coefficient_results |>
  select(
    term,
    estimate,
    std.error,
    conf.low,
    conf.high,
    p.value
  ) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(
    term = "Predictor",
    estimate = "Estimate",
    std.error = "SE",
    conf.low = "95% CI lower",
    conf.high = "95% CI upper",
    p.value = "p"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(
      estimate,
      std.error,
      conf.low,
      conf.high
    ),
    decimals = 3
  ) |>
  fmt(
    columns = p.value,
    fns = function(x) {
      ifelse(
        x < .001,
        "< .001",
        sprintf("%.3f", x)
      )
    }
  )
```
```{r, selected model performance}

selected_row |>
  select(
    Model,
    AIC,
    BIC,
    logLik,
    deviance,
    df.residual,
    Nested.df,
    Nested.Chisq.stat,
    Nested.p.value
  ) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(
    Model = "Model",
    AIC = "AIC",
    BIC = "BIC",
    logLik = "Log-likelihood",
    deviance = "Deviance",
    df.residual = "Residual df",
    Nested.df = "Nested df",
    Nested.Chisq.stat = "Nested χ²",
    Nested.p.value = "Nested p"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = where(is.numeric),
    decimals = 2
  )
```
### Coefficients are on the log-odds scale

```{r, fixed f}
fixef(mod3)
```

The coefficients represent changes in the log-odds of surviving the Titanic crash, holding the other predictors constant.

Holding ticket class and age constant, the **log-odds** of survival were `r round(fixef(mod3)$cond[["Sex.Binary"]], 2)` higher for female passengers than for male passengers.

The coefficients for `Pclass2` and `Pclass3` represent **log-odds differences** relative to first-class passengers, our reference group. Holding sex and age constant, the log-odds of survival were `r round(abs(fixef(mod3)$cond[["Pclass2"]]), 2)` lower for second-class passengers and `r round(abs(fixef(mod3)$cond[["Pclass3"]]), 2)` lower for third-class passengers than for first-class passengers.

For each one-year increase in age, holding sex and ticket class constant, the **log-odds** of survival decrease by `r round(abs(fixef(mod3)$cond[["Age"]]), 3)`.

### Transform log-odds into odds ratios

```{r, orexp}
exp(fixef(mod3)$cond)
```

```{r, or ci}
or_ci <- exp(confint(mod3, parm = "beta_"))
or_ci
```

### Interpreting sex

Holding ticket class and age constant, female passengers had `r round(exp(fixef(mod3)$cond[["Sex.Binary"]]), 2)` times the odds of surviving compared to male passengers, 95% CI \[`r round(or_ci["Sex.Binary", 1], 2)`, `r round(or_ci["Sex.Binary", 2], 2)`\].

### Interpreting ticket class

Holding sex and age constant, second-class passengers had `r round(exp(fixef(mod3)$cond[["Pclass2"]]), 2)` times the odds of surviving compared to first-class passengers, 95% CI \[`r round(or_ci["Pclass2", 1], 2)`, `r round(or_ci["Pclass2", 2], 2)`\], and third-class passengers had `r round(exp(fixef(mod3)$cond[["Pclass3"]]), 2)` times the odds, 95% CI \[`r round(or_ci["Pclass3", 1], 2)`, `r round(or_ci["Pclass3", 2], 2)`\].

### Interpreting age

Holding sex and ticket class constant, each one-year increase in age is associated with `r round(exp(fixef(mod3)$cond[["Age"]]), 2)` times the odds of surviving, 95% CI \[`r round(or_ci["Age", 1], 2)`, `r round(or_ci["Age", 2], 2)`\].

#### Age

```{r, pred age}
#| fig-height: 2.8

pred_age <- ggpredict(mod3, terms = "Age [0:80 by=1]")

ggplot(pred_age, aes(x, predicted)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), alpha = 0.18) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(
    x = "Age (years)",
    y = "Predicted Probability of Survival"
  ) +
  theme_classic()
```


> We fit a binomial GLM with a logit link predicting survival of the Titanic crash from sex, ticket class, and age. Female passengers had higher odds of surviving than male passengers, OR = `r round(exp(fixef(mod3)$cond[["Sex.Binary"]]), 2)`, 95% CI \[`r round(or_ci["Sex.Binary", 1], 2)`, `r round(or_ci["Sex.Binary", 2], 2)`\]. Compared to first-class passengers, second-class passengers had lower odds of surviving, OR = `r round(exp(fixef(mod3)$cond[["Pclass2"]]), 2)`, 95% CI \[`r round(or_ci["Pclass2", 1], 2)`, `r round(or_ci["Pclass2", 2], 2)`\], as did third-class passengers, OR = `r round(exp(fixef(mod3)$cond[["Pclass3"]]), 2)`, 95% CI \[`r round(or_ci["Pclass3", 1], 2)`, `r round(or_ci["Pclass3", 2], 2)`\]. Older passengers had lower odds of surviving, OR = `r round(exp(fixef(mod3)$cond[["Age"]]), 2)`, 95% CI \[`r round(or_ci["Age", 1], 2)`, `r round(or_ci["Age", 2], 2)`\], per additional year of age.

## 6. Discussing Findings and Limitations
These results suggest that sex was the most important factor in surviving the Titanic crash. Women had more than twelve times the odds of survival of men with the same ticket class and age, as expected because of the “women and children first” saying. Ticket class was the second most important factor: compared with first-class passengers, second-class passengers had 1/4th of the odds of survival, and third-class passengers had 1/10th of the odds, suggesting that socioeconomic status affected access to the lifeboats. Age had the smallest but still meaningful effect, with each additional year reducing the odds of survival by about 4%, which is consistent with children being given some priority.

Limitations: The analysis excluded 177 passengers with missing age, and if age was more often missing for certain groups (for example, third-class passengers), the results may not fully represent all passengers. Some recorded ages were estimates, and age was modelled as a linear effect, although the diagnostics hinted that survival may not decline steadily with age, for example if young children were prioritized more strongly than a linear trend implies. Finally, because these data are observational, the results show who was more likely to survive but cannot establish why; for example, the class effect may be more about preferential treatment than cabin location-- we don't know where everyone was during the crash.
